title: Legal profession: Occupational boundaries shape perceived expertise
desc: Frames legal practice as socially differentiated and empirically bounded, measuring lawyers’ attitudes rather than contemporary task substitutability or market change.

kps.k: The cluster frames legal practice as socially differentiated, rather than as a single, uniform occupation.
kps.d: Chicago Lawyers: The Social Structure of the Bar compares specialties through client type, corporate-client income, relationship continuity, client volume, court appearances and organisational setting. It also measures educational and social background and perceived prestige. Its contribution is a framework for examining differences across the bar, not a demonstrated causal account of those differences. A practical implication is to distinguish client markets and practice settings when assessing claims about changes to legal work.

kps.k: The study treats expertise and occupational boundaries as matters for empirical inquiry, while measuring lawyers' perceptions rather than task substitutability.
kps.d: Respondents contrast specialised with broad practice, advisory and negotiating skills with technical procedures, and work requiring lawyers with work trained paraprofessionals could perform. They also report whether other occupations encroach on their work. These contrasts identify potential lines of disagreement about professional expertise; they do not establish which tasks nonlawyers can perform or how widely respondents hold each view. They provide no direct evidence about AI capabilities or displacement.

kps.k: Bar-association attitudes connect professional improvement with protection of occupational boundaries.
kps.d: The tables separately examine the perceived importance and effectiveness of objectives including continuing education, judicial improvement, discipline, member services, public standing and preventing nonlawyers from doing legal work. These are surveyed attitudes, not author-endorsed recommendations. They distinguish what lawyers want professional associations to do from how well they think associations perform, but corrupted table alignment prevents reliable claims about which groups disagree.

kps.k: The available material supports a descriptive framework, not dependable numerical findings or contemporary market conclusions.
kps.d: Severe OCR corruption limits interpretation of Chicago Lawyers. Its methods also require care: reported time allocation defines practice fields, sparse fields are consolidated or excluded, missing responses change table bases, and some categories receive assigned values rather than direct answers. Readers should therefore avoid numerical rankings and causal conclusions from these excerpts. The supplied Robin AI material contains no interpretable substantive content; its title alone cannot establish staffing or fundraising claims.

vlens.an: The sole supplied source-level record for this professional voice contains no interpretable substantive content. It therefore provides no reliable basis for determining whether market analysts, consultancies and press accept, extend, redirect or oppose the proposition that legal practice is socially differentiated and empirically bounded, with perceived expertise shaped by occupational boundaries. Because the corpus is curated rather than representative, this evidentiary gap should not be generalized to the wider professional voice.

The academia-and-research source supports the proposition by treating legal practice as socially differentiated across specialties, client types and organisational settings, and by examining expertise and occupational boundaries through lawyers’ reported perceptions. It also reinforces the proposition’s limits: the survey does not demonstrate contemporary task substitutability, AI capability or market change, and its methodological qualifications—compounded by severe OCR corruption—preclude confident numerical or causal conclusions. Internal variation lies mainly in the dimensions the study asks respondents to assess, including specialised versus broad practice, advisory versus technical work, and lawyer-exclusive versus paraprofessional-capable tasks; however, the available material cannot reliably establish how particular respondent groups divide on those questions. Because this facet contains one curated source, it should not be read as representing academic or research opinion generally.

elens.an: The pre-2015 source supports the proposition by treating legal practice as socially differentiated across specialties, client types, practice settings and professional backgrounds, rather than as a uniform occupation. It also examines expertise and occupational boundaries through lawyers’ reported views about specialisation, paraprofessional capability and encroachment by other occupations. Material variation lies in what the evidence can establish: it maps respondents’ perceptions and organisational differences but does not demonstrate actual task substitutability, explain those differences causally or support conclusions about contemporary AI-driven market change. Methodological qualifications—including category construction, missing responses and sparse fields—together with severe OCR corruption further limit dependable numerical comparisons. Because this facet contains one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of all foundational scholarship.

The sole supplied source-level record for the 2025 period contains no interpretable substantive content. It therefore provides no reliable basis for determining whether the source accepts, extends, redirects or rejects the proposition that legal practice is socially differentiated and that occupational boundaries shape perceived expertise. In particular, it offers no evidence about differences among legal specialties, lawyers’ perceptions of tasks that nonlawyers could perform, protection of professional boundaries, or contemporary task substitutability and market change. Because this is a curated source selection rather than a survey, this absence of usable evidence should not be generalized to 2025 sources or treated as evidence about the prevalence of any position.
